newsitem.title: USA: Ford's U.S. sales fall 2.6 pct, Toyota's up 5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Ford's U.S. sales fall 2.6 pct, Toyota's up 5 pct.

text.p: Capping a strong automotive market in March, Ford Motor Co. Thursday reported a 2.6 percent drop in light vehicle sales, while red-hot Toyota Motor Corp. posted a 5 percent gain.

Americans bought cars and trucks at an annualized rate of 15.8 million units in March, up from 15.5 million a year earlier and 15.3 million in February -- an indication of continued strength in the market.
Total industry sales in March were up 1.4 percent to 1,396,392 light vehicles. For the first quarter of 1997, sales were up 2 percent to 3,642,288 units.
But Ford reported weakness in passenger car demand, with sales North American-built cars down 9.5 percent from a year earlier to 141,305 units.

Ford's light truck sales, which include the strong-selling pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles that have powered most of the company's automotive profits in recent years, rose 3.5 percent to 201,142 units.

Detroit's No. 2 automaker said its first-quarter North American truck output was a record, up 8 percent over last year, despite a strike at a truck seat supplier. It predicted that second-quarter truck output would be up 10 percent over the year-ago period, leading to another record.

"We've expanded our truck assembly capacity substantially in recent years and presently nearly all of our truck plants are operating on overtime schedules to keep pace with strong consumer demand," the No. 2 U.S. automaker said.
But Ford said some of its key car models posted declines, including the Taurus, which dropped 9.1 percent, and the Contour, which fell 16 percent.

At the end of the first quarter, the Taurus, with sales of 88,135 units, had relinquished its position as America's best-selling car to the Chevrolet Cavalier, which had sales of 91,189. Toyota's Camry was the third-best seller.
Overall, Ford sold 345,065 light vehicles in March, versus 354,105 a year earlier.

Toyota's sales, which posted double-digit increases in January and February, cooled to 121,751 units, 5 percent above the year-ago period. Toyota's domestic car sales rose 4.1 percent, but the big story was import trucks, with sales of new entries such as the RAV4 and 4Runner sport utility vehicles up 23 percent.
General Motors Corp. on Wednesday reported a 4.1 percent sales increase, due partly to new models and the fact that March 1996 truck sales were dragged down by a costly strike.
